synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a ground conflict during taxiout at MIA airport resulting in an aircraft having to execute a go-around.
narrative: Contacted MIA ground for taxi. Controller advised expect Rwy 8L for takeoff and to taxi via Txy K to holding point for Rwy 8L.  We had loaded Rwy 8R during preflight; so during the taxi; I loaded Rwy 8L; entered the takeoff data; and confirmed waypoints.  The CA called for the Runway Change checklist and it was completed halfway to the holding point.  Ground then directed us to monitor Tower frequency approaching the holding point.  When tower contacted us; they directed us to cross runway 8L and hold short Rwy 8R and expedite for traffic on 5-mile final. As we crossed the hold short line for Rwy 8L; tower advised us to proceed onto hold for Rwy 8R.  I advised that we would need a few minutes to run checklists.  Tower replied with hold short Rwy 8L and the CA applied brakes; but we were past the hold short line by about 50 feet.  I advised tower and he said to then expedite and hold short Rwy 8R; traffic on 2 mile final. CA advanced throttles; but we did not clear Rwy 8L in time and traffic on final was directed to Go Around.  Holding Short of Rwy 8R we completed all the runway change items one last time and rest of departure was uneventful.Cause: Change of Runway assignment followed by expedited instructions to cross and then on to the new runway and hold before crew could run required checklists.  I also should have been more vocal about our requirements before attempting to cross Rwy 8L; but with the hold short instructions initially provided for the other side; I thought we would have time while holding short of Rwy 8R.Suggestions: When workload is high and expedited instructions are received to cross an active runway; request hold short of that runway to ensure all requirements are completed to prevent conflicts.
secondary_narrative: Our preflight was normal.  We had the aircraft set up for a departure off of runway 08R and also had the numbers for 08L.  We blocked out early.  Upon receiving initial Taxi clearance we were told to taxi via K to runway 08L and expect 08L for departure.  We immediately reconfigured the aircraft for 08L and had the runway change checklist completed before crossing taxiway K7.  Around approximately taxiway Z the ground controller had us switch to tower and monitor.  We were approximately abeam the beginning of taxiway K1 when the tower controller said 'Aircraft X; cross runway 08L hold short runway 08R traffic five miles out I need you to expedite.' We proceeded to cross 08L and were waiting to reconfigure for 08R until we were stopped and holding short of 08R.  All numbers and  power settings were exactly the same.  We had discussed and noted this before initial taxi. We just had to select runway 08R; reenter V speeds;  and repeat the runway change checklist. As we were crossing the runway 08L hold short line the tower controller said 'Aircraft X Line up and wait runway 08R.'  We responded we'd need a minute to change the numbers and run the checklist.  The controller then said 'Aircraft X hold short  runway 08L.' We responded 'Unable we have already crossed the hold short line.'  The tower controller then said 'Then I need you to expedite crossing 08L and hold short 08R traffic two mile final.' We had stopped when he initially told us to hold short and were now trying to expedite again. At that moment I immediately observed the aircraft on final begin their go around.Cause: When receiving our initial taxi clearance the controller initially gave us 08R then said 'hold on ….'  there was about a three to five second pause then he came back and said 'Taxi via K to runway 08L.'  I believe during that pause the ground controller likely checked with the tower controller or someone else and asked if it was ok to give us 08L. We did not ask for this however I think they were just trying to be accommodating. I think there was some sort of miscommunication between ground and tower and that translated into the tower controller giving us 08R when the ground controller had given us 08L.  In the moment the tower controller got audibly agitated with us as I felt he thought we weren't prepared.  In reality we were fully prepared for either runway and were set up for the runway given.  I just should have refused to cross runway 08L at the initial instruction until we were fully set up again.  In past experience I have also had them do almost the same thing previously to me. The previous time I stopped prior to 08L; reconfigured for 08R; then they eventually came back and reassigned us back to 08L prior to takeoff.Suggestions: In hindsight when the controller initially issued a runway different than we were expecting I should have just held short of runway 08L and told him we were going to have to change numbers and run the runway change checklist there.  I was trying to make it work in the wrong place.  Going forward I that's what I will do.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported SFO Runways 1L and 1R do not have hold short lines due to ongoing construction and a tug was observed driving right to the edge of Runway 28L during takeoff roll.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported a traffic conflict on final approach with an aircraft on the runway resulting in an ATC directed go-around. The go-around resulted in an undesired aircraft state before regaining aircraft control and a return for another approach and landing.
narrative: A complex go-around created by an ATC landing/take-off conflict led to an undesired aircraft state in which the PM perceived safety was in jeopardy and took control of the aircraft.The flight began eventfully with a passenger and service animal issue that caused a delayed departure. Once resolved; the taxi out through initial approach was unremarkable. The workload and complexity began during the latter stages of the arrival and clearance for the approach.The weather was approximately OVERCAST010 to FEW050 and there was a NOTAM for our landing runway (XXR) that advised 'Special Authorization Cat 1 (ILS) procedure Not Authorized; unless advised by ATC that cranes are down.' As we were cleared for the approach and above the glideslope (~2000' AGL); I directed the PM to inquire on the status of the cranes. We were informed multiple times that the 'cranes are up' and there was an unfamiliarity from ATC about this NOTAM; but eventually a declaration that 'we are authorized for the approach.' Meanwhile; I had disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle; accelerating about five knots; but intercepted the glideslope configured gear/F15; slowing from 165kts to target speed at the FAF/1500' AGL. We briefly discussed that we felt safe continuing the approach; completing the landing checklist prior to 1000' AGL and entering IMC. This phase was the first element of complexity during this approach.Upon breaking out of the weather at approximately 800' AGL; I observed an airplane on the runway and queried the PM if he saw the same thing. He confirmed there was an airplane there; followed by ATC providing instructions to it and the preceding aircraft. Next; we verified stable at 500' AGL and were discussing the probability of a go-around as the aircraft was slow to begin the takeoff roll. ATC instructed us to go around at approximately 300' AGL; but with noticeable closure on the impending lift-off of the other aircraft. I initiated the go around in accordance with the SOP; while offsetting to the right (away from the other runway) and remaining under the weather layer; keeping the departing aircraft in sight. I was unable to verify any of the PM go-around actions as I was primarily concerned about flightpath deconfliction with the other aircraft and verbally said 'what does he want us to do' as I estimated our distance to the other aircraft nearing 3000' nose-tail separation. ATC then gave us a left turn to 060 (nearly across the taking off aircraft's flight path) and climb to 3000' MSL; and after a slight delay; I complied with that instruction; beginning the climb back into IMC. This phase was the second element of complexity during this approach.As we climbed into the weather and I transitioned to instruments; I observed the aircraft passing through approximately 1200' MSL at approximately 12 degrees nose high pitch; but with an airspeed of approximately 190 KIAS and decreasing rapidly with the trend arrow approaching 160 KIAS. I immediately lowered the nose towards 5 degrees nose high as I scanned across the other side of the cockpit to analyze the poor aircraft performance. During this time; I believe I said '(check) Flaps' or possibly 'level change; set Climb Speed (CMS); Flaps 5;' but more attention was narrowly focused on determining the throttle setting/engine performance and aircraft gear/flap configuration. I continued to lower the flight path towards level flight; advanced the throttles slightly; and did observe increasing airspeed; as well as a momentary sink rate of approximately 500' FPM. There was comm from both ATC and the PM during this point that I did not fully interpret while focused on precisely controlling the flight path; while also still attempting to diagnose the performance degradation. At this point; without any Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) aural warnings; the PM perceived 'red terrain' on the Navigation Display and said 'climb' and then 'I have the aircraft.' Obviously; this was also startling; but I released control of the aircraft and tried to make the mental shift to gain Situational Awareness (SA) as the new PM. I did not immediately notice any 'red terrain'; but did perceive a significant increase in pitch attitude. Still without certainty of the flap position; I begin moving the flaps to a lower setting; neither the FO nor I can definitively say who moved the flaps to 5; though we know he did press LVL Change and set CMS at some point in this immediate sequence of transitioning PF/PM roles. While still gaining SA; I observed 'yellow terrain' on our nose starting at approximately five nautical miles and made a request to ATC that 'we need a turn away.' ATC subsequently provided a frequency change; the new PF also said things during this time that I did not fully comprehend. I observed the aircraft continuing to accelerate; nearing 250 knots and I raised the flaps to UP; the 'FLAPS; FLAPS' aural warning also sounded at some point during this sequence of me functioning as the PM. The PF at some point engaged Command B and we cleared the weather back into VMC. This phase was the third element of complexity during this approach.Now on top of the weather with a stable aircraft and on a good vector and altitude; we were able to restore normal CRM; and executed the after take-off checklist. We double checked each other and the aircraft; returned to the original PF/PM roles; completed a descent check; and uneventful landing and taxi-in (though there was still concern/uncertainty regarding the NOTAMs referencing the cranes; but we had not noticed any on the previous approach).  Due to being late; we only very briefly debriefed in the airplane after completing the parking checklist and I said we would discuss prior to the next flight. The FO left the jet as I stayed to wish passengers farewell and apologize again for the inconvenience. Upon exiting; I saw the CA of the next flight on the jetbridge and we discussed the passenger service animal and NOTAM issue for several minutes. I arrived to the next aircraft and began a deliberate debrief with the FO; recognizing that we will probably be late departing. During our discussions; it became apparent to me that we may have oversped the flaps; I then left the middle of our debrief to go back to the other aircraft to inform the Captain of our suspicion; stating that it was less than 10 knots; for less than 10 seconds; at Flaps 5 or less at ~2000' MSL. I returned to satisfactorily continue our debrief; double checking on the fitness of both the FO and my own fitness for duty for the next flight. He stated that he was; I agreed with his assessment; and did not have concerns regarding my fitness. The next flight was conducted uneventfully.To recap and summarize; the slightly varied and out-of-sync SA among the PF; PM; and ATC resulted in multiple missed/delayed comm and lack of shared mental model on the flight deck (degraded CRM); ultimately producing a poorly executed go around.

The PA30 announced a 2-mile Final; the Cessna pilots visually scanned the final approach; did not see traffic and immediately proceeded towards the runway for departure. The Cessna pilot immediately stopped the aircraft approximately 150 feet from the runway edge but beyond the hold short line. The left seat pilot looked again; saw the PA30 and judged the aircraft to be about 1 inch wide on the windscreen. The pilots exchange dialogue for a few moments to verify positions; and eventually the PA30 executed a go-around  which seemed to be several hundred feet above the threshold; Contributing factors: Overcast; grey sky; and Cessna was position perpendicular to the departing runway. It may have been possible to see the PA30's landing lights.Human Factors: Cessna crew was alert; fatigue was not a factor. synopsis: Citation Latitude Captain reported a traffic conflict with an aircraft on downwind when crossing the hold short line at a non-towered airport.
narrative: We were holding short of runway XX at ZZZ on the east side of the runway. We had just received an IFR release from air traffic control who gave us a three minute void time. There was one aircraft on downwind for runway XX. We made a radio call to the common traffic advisory frequency to advise that we were going to take the runway for departure. As we began to power up past the hold short line; the first officer said stop stop. I stopped the aircraft with the nose just passed the hold short line for runway XX at the approach end. As I looked over the shoulder of my first officer towards the 3 o'clock of our airplane; I saw a C130 approaching low and fast on a severely short approach. The C130 operator had not advised us of his intention to make a short approach. Due to the close proximity and high approach speed of the C130 I chose to stop and remain where we were and advise the C130 our nose was just passed the hold short line. The C130 made a radio call on the common traffic advisory frequency to say they were on left base. In the interest of safety and out of an abundance of caution; I chose to allow the C130 to execute his procedure first before taking the runway. The C130 accomplished a touch and go in front of us and then afterwards we departed without incident.Suggestions: It's incredibly important; especially in an uncontrolled airport environment to be aware of the type of aircraft sharing the airspace. This particular C130 was a firefighting tanker out doing practice maneuvers. The aircraft commander of the C130 never indicated to us the type of aircraft they were or the nature of their fighter pilot type of approach that they were planning on accomplishing. The aircraft descended very quickly from 1600 feet above the runway on a downwind in a hard left bank straight to the runway threshold. This type of approach caught us off guard as we assumed a normal approaching landing which would have given us more than enough time to depart safely without conflict. I'm thankful to the first officer for having his head on a swivel and calling out the closure rate of the surprise maneuver.

synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported a non-communicating aircraft entered the opposite end of the runway while landing; resulting in a critical ground conflict.
narrative: At just past XA:00 on Day 0 I was returning from ZZZ to LOM and requested RNAV 6 from PHL Approach Control (123.8) for practicing my IFR flow (the field was visual). A request that was accepted by PHL Approach. I was directed to the LASBE (IAF-RNAV 6) and cleared for the approach. On turning to the final approach course; I told PHL approach that I had visual of the field. They advised me that there was no traffic observed. At this time; I canceled my IFR. I switched to CTAF and made a 9-mile final call on the CTAF; followed by a 5-mile final call; followed by a short final call. I did a quick scan of the runway on short final; and everything looked good to land.As I touched down; I see a plane on 24 at the opposite end of the runway; and that is the first time I heard him. His call was to warn me of his presence on the runway. He had just rolled on to 24 and was fortunately stationary at that end. There was no danger of any collision since I stopped within 1500 feet or so of touchdown and taxied off the runway. Once the runway was clear; the other plane departed as soon as I was off the runway. When I walked into the FBO (there is a speaker tuned to CTAF); the people there told me that they heard my 3rd call - the short final call; but not the first two (or did not pay attention). They said they never heard the other plane till he piped up to warn me of his presence when I had already touched down and I was on my landing roll. What did I learn? When I am on a short final; I am generally focused on the touch down point; typically the numbers at LOM; and once I pass the threshold and begin my level out and flare is when I raise my eyes to the end of the runway. I think that is what I did on this landing as well and by the time the presence of the plane at the other end registered with me; I was on the ground and slowing down. It was too late to go around. I should not assume that the runway is mine even if I have been making calls; scanning and hearing nothing on the radio. I should always be more watchful and continue scanning the entire runway environment; including at this late stage in my landings.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported LHW has unlit signs that are improperly located and the pavement markings are faded.
narrative: On Day 0; I taxied to take off from Runway 33 LHW in Georgia. The hold short line is extremely faded; and is several hundred feet from the beginning of the runway. I overstepped it by about an airplane length. I stopped; called the Tower and apologized. The Tower cleared me for takeoff and instructed me to turn right to a heading less than one mile after Departure End of Runway (DER). I was distracted by the passing of the line; the non-standard takeoff procedure; but believed all was OK.Immediately after takeoff; when I looked at the engine parameters screen; I noticed something was unusual; but it was not immediately clear what that was - all indicators were in the green; but something seemed different than my usual picture. I was already in the air; committed to completing the takeoff; and under the instructions of very short turn clearance. I continued the climb and planned on identifying the issue and dealing with it once stabilized on the climb; after the turn; however; at that point I turned left instead of right. The Tower directed my attention to the issue but gracefully said that there was no need to correct.The irregularity turned out to be higher than normal oil temperature indication. Once that was clear; I performed a precautionary landing. It was an incorrect indication problem.Lessons and conclusion: The initial hold short line crossing was irregular and got me a bit unsettled; and worried about consequences. In conjunction with the irregular indication; I made the second mistake. The conclusion is that I must make sure that I am 100% back to myself before accepting a clearance.Another lesson is that the markings (throughout the field) in LHW are truly bad; and in my mind at an unacceptable level. Signs are unlit; pavement markings are very faded; and the location of signs is improper. I would like to suggest that placing hold-short line locations on taxi diagrams is a good idea; especially when the hold-short line is so far from the actual runway (I estimate at least 250 ft.). I think that the average pilot will look for a hold-short line much closer to the runway and when the line is so faded will easily miss it. This however clearly does not release me from missing it.

synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter on final approach at a non-towered airport. The helicopter landed in front of the pilot on the same runway; no damage occurred.
narrative: There has been a good deal of helicopter training here over the last few years. Generally we never have a problem with the helicopters; as they try to account for the normal traffic here and are rarely a problem. Mind you; I'm not necessarily blaming the helicopter here; just trying to give some background about our particular airport.I made the usual radio calls at 10 and 5 miles; and I was following a Cirrus in about as closely as prudent. There was a helicopter making right traffic above us; and he seemed to be a new guy; but we were all making the appropriate calls. Because of the fact that I was hundreds of feet lower; had clearly announced final at a mile and a half out; and the helicopters are usually good about waiting for us to pass; I thought all was well. But he did descend fairly quickly; and landed on our end of the runway instead of the far end at about the same time I did.I thought it might be unwise to go around; since a helicopter could do almost anything. I always land at the start of the runway in a short distance -- since I always make the first turn-off -- so I did that; but did get a nasty comment from a pilot flying overhead. I don't think he was particularly blaming me. But I didn't like how it played out really; and I said at the time that it was probably my fault to mollify him.If you go by who is in front; well yes; he's a helicopter and he turned in front of me. If you go by who is lower; then I was. I think that I should have gotten a direct answer from him instead of just assuming that he was waiting for us both to land; but I was working with the Cirrus so closely on the radio that I didn't think he would try to get in between us.The safety lesson? Be careful around students? I'm not entirely sure; since I'm still thinking about it. I have always held that the helicopters have just as much of a right to be here as we do; but then again; they've been very considerate too. In this case; I probably figured that I had made radio calls and they would do as usual; and they probably figured that since they had made previous radio calls; it was all good.

synopsis: General aviation pilot crew reported a near collision on the takeoff roll with an aircraft taking off on the crossing runway at a non-towered airport. The Captain delayed the rotation to avoid the other aircraft.
narrative: While operating a passenger flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we planned a departure on RW XX with a right forward quartering headwind /crosswind. We taxied to runway XX and announced our intentions on the Unicom frequency. We received our IFR clearance on the ground via ZZZ CTR on the radio as well.We heard no other traffic on the Unicom frequency of XXX.XX We saw no visible traffic during our taxi; in the air or on the ground. The Cessna 182 had taxied much earlier than us so assumed he had departed on his flight to ZZZ2. There were no radio transmissions from the Cessna 182 and that was confirmed via the FBO audio recorded during that time period.Our transmissions were on the recording stating our intentions to taxi to RW XX. We completed our taxi check and were holding short of RW XX. The Co-pilot transmitted our departure intentions for ZZZ RW XX and we began our normal takeoff roll. The aircraft accelerated normally and the Co-Pilot called V1 and Rotate; At that moment the C182 appeared at about 11 o clock in the windshield and approximately 50 to 75 ft. in the air. It was too late for an aborted takeoff as it appeared we would pass barely underneath the the C182. A rotation at that instant would have caused impact with the C182. I felt the safest option was to delay the rotation and remain on the runway for a couple of seconds as the traffic passed over us. It happened very quickly and we rotated and resumed the climb away from the runway. The remainder of the flight was normal and uneventful. The incident occurred due to lack of situational awareness resulting from a lack of radio communication. I was unaware visually of another aircraft positioned at RW XY prior to beginning the takeoff roll. This incident could have been avoided by pilots verifying correct Unicom/ CTAF frequencies in use at uncontrolled airports. Visually verifying other aircraft when possible and the use of all available appropriate aircraft lighting to enhance visibility.
secondary_narrative: Our aircraft was departing on runway XX. I made CTAF calls taxiing out of the FBO via 1 and made a call once on runway XX ready for takeoff. Another aircraft was seen taxiing on the other side of the airfield via taxiway 2. No radio calls were heard from that aircraft. Visual contact was lost as it blended in to the airport environment at the approach end of runway XY. We started our takeoff roll and as we passed V1 speeds we visually saw the other aircraft departing runway XY. It was approximately 75-100 ft. AGL as it passed directly over us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. We elected to stay on the ground/runway at takeoff speed until the overflying aircraft was not a factor overhead. We then executed our takeoff with sufficient runway left to safely get airborne.Once airborne at approximately 1000 feet AGL I made another call on CTAF that we were turning northbound and departing the airport environment. No response was heard from any other aircraft in the area; including the aircraft we narrowly missed.Once landed at our destination in ZZZ1 we called airport personnel via cell phone to determine if they could hear our calls on the radio. They returned our call the next morning and stated that they heard ALL of our radio calls but none from the other aircraft. We had briefly talked with the other aircraft's pilot/occupant and knew that they were heading to ZZZ2. We called company at ZZZ2 and determined the aircraft's identification to be Aircraft Y. We did not make any contact with the crew of Aircraft Y as they had left the airfield.We believe that Aircraft Y may have been on the wrong CTAF frequency in ZZZ which is why we did not hear any radio transmissions from them nor did airport personnel. If true this directly caused the problem. To prevent this from happening again; we should have attempted to make direct radio contact with the other aircraft we saw taxiing either on CTAF or Guard frequency. If no contact made; we should have delayed taking our runway until we could absolutely confirm that other aircraft had taken off from their runway and was no longer a hazard.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported taking the runway for departure with an airplane on short final. Reporter stated the other aircraft was not communicating its intentions.
narrative: Takeoff RWY 35 BDN. As the aircraft departing ahead became airborne; and visually clearing the final approach course; I crossed the runway hold short line and announced on CTAF; 'Taking RWY 35 for westbound departure.' Approximately 30 feet after crossing the hold short line another aircraft announced on CTAF; 'We're on short final.' I came to a complete stop; other aircraft announced going around. On CTAF I advised we'd heard no radio call and did not observe the other aircraft. Other aircraft responded; 'I made three calls.' There was also some mention on frequency of a 'dogleg final.' I never saw the other aircraft until it was established on downwind after its go around. In my aircraft there were three (3) pilots; with a cumulative total of 35000+ hours.  All of us were monitoring CTAF and no one heard a call from the other aircraft.Suggested remedies: Although radios are not required at non-towered airports; good procedure would be to make a call on CTAF/UNICOM and then pause for possible responses BEFORE crossing the hold short onto the runway. At non-towered airports; with other traffic observed on the ground and in the pattern; aircraft should fly a standard pattern so that they can be observed when on final approach.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a runway incursion after confusing an ATC clearance to line up and wait after arriving aircraft.
narrative: Flight number: ABCD / ZZZ-ZZZZAt XA:07; ZZZ parking position was 1. Taxi clearance was received from Tower to taxi via 1 across Runway XX and continue via 2-3 to Runway XX. (Clearance from the tower was obtained to taxi via 1 across Runway XX and continue along 2-3.) The aircraft taxied out via 1-2-3 to Runway XX.At XA:14; the tower cleared the preceding aircraft for takeoff.At XA:16; the tower instructed: 'Aircraft X; cleared Runway XX line up and wait after arrival.'At approximately XA:15 at ZZZ; Aircraft Y was on short final for Runway XX.As CM2; I read back: 'Line up and wait Runway XX; Aircraft X.' Approximately one second later; I added: 'Line up behind; Aircraft X.' No correction or clarification was provided by ATC following either readback at the time.In a dynamic runway environment at ZZZ Runway XX; the crew's actions; including runway entry during the rollout phase; were based on real-time interpretation of the received transmission and a visual scan of the runway environment.After establishing position on the Runway XX centerline; the preceding aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. Tower then instructed the subsequent arriving aircraft to go around and advised that our runway entry was not authorized. We were subsequently instructed to vacate Runway XX via Taxiway 4 at ZZZ. The event was subsequently classified as a runway incursion.Contributing Factors (Human Factors)Contributing factors included ambiguity in the timing structure of the clearance phraseology ('line up and wait after arrival') in the context of operations on Runway XX at ZZZ; requiring real-time interpretation in a dynamic runway environment.VHF communication characteristics and associated audio conditions may have resulted in perceived audio degradation and reduced intelligibility of the transmission. Post-event review of recorded ATC communications was conducted using a high-fidelity audio playback system with slowed playback to enhance intelligibility. This review suggested that portions of the transmission may have been subject to audio degradation during high cockpit workload conditions; resulting in reduced transmission intelligibility.The flight crew independently perceived the transmission in real time as a Line Up and Wait-related clearance.The absence of ATC correction to two separate readbacks may have reinforced the crew's understanding of the transmission.At the ZZZ Runway XX 3 intersection; runway guard lights were available as the primary visual cue; and no runway stop bar system was present. The available lighting configuration provided limited additional visual confirmation or redundancy for runway entry verification between ATC and flight crews. This may have reduced an additional layer of defence that could otherwise assist in resolving ambiguity or reinforcing runway entry status during high-tempo operations.Safety Actions TakenContinuous traffic monitoring was maintained prior to runway entry at ZZZ Runway XX. No evasive maneuver was required during the event; and no collision or loss of separation occurred.Corrective Action / PreventionIn future operations at ZZZ; greater emphasis will be placed on positive confirmation of runway status prior to entering a runway under LUAW clearances; particularly when sequencing is referenced in conjunction with arriving traffic.Enhanced cross-checking of ATC instructions between crew members will be reinforced to mitigate potential interpretation divergence. Additional awareness will be maintained regarding VHF communication degradation and the importance of seeking explicit clarification when any ambiguity exists in runway-related clearances.

synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported the markings and signage at Taxiway Delta and Runway 30/12 at TUS are confusing and can lead to runway and taxiway incursions.
narrative: I was cleared for a straight in landing on runway 22 due to approaching the airport from the east. The active runway at the time for other arrivals was runway 12. I have flown to TUS a lot in the past. Normally after touchdown tower will instruct me to do a 180 on the runway and back taxi to alpha and contact ground / proceed to the FBO. Or sometimes I will be instructed to make a left on delta 3 and contact ground. In this case the controller was busy transmitting to another aircraft by the time I had slowed down so I made the first available exit which happened to be taxiway alpha 2. After vacating onto alpha 2 I realized I was now directly in the approach path / area of runway 12 with Aircraft Y on a few mile final for this very runway. I decided to hang another left and get clear of the area on taxiway delta to prevent a problem before contacting tower who then handed me off to ground. The ground controller did not mention anything about an incursion and instructed me to taxi along delta to the ramp as usual.The situation still felt weird to me after the fact however because while I taxied on delta to the ramp I crossed over a red marking on the pavement that said 30-12" that would imply I was just on an active runway without a clearance even though the taxiway turnoff that brought me here didn't say anything. After looking through other safety reports I am not the first person to get confused by the taxiway layout at this specific intersection despite having lots of experience operating here. When you are rolling out on runway 22 taxiway alpha 2 looks like a completely normal turn off. No special markings on the runway and no red signs for an intersecting runway approaching. Alpha 2 is also depicted like any other taxiway on the airport diagram on initial glance. Once you are on alpha 2 however you are on runway 12 and that becomes apparent when you vacate runway 22 and now see runway 12 right in front of you. When you then make either a left or right onto delta you cross over a pair of hold bars that read in red letters on the concrete "30-12" again implying you are / were on a runway even though the taxi diagram depicts it as a taxiway and there are yellow stripe markings on the ground. Upon review after the situation it appears this is known as a "aligned taxiway" which the FAA has since prohibited being used for new construction or reconstruction of taxiways presumably because it confuses pilots. There is currently a hot spot on the airport diagram for one side of the intersection however it does not mention the above scenario but instead only acknowledges that pilots tend to cross the hold markings when taxiing to runway 12 via delta presumably due to the uncommon layout of the intersection.I believe that something design wise visually needs to change at this intersection to prevent future issues and needless pilot deviations as in the case of some other safety reports. Pilots are misinterpreting the existing markings and signage and the airport diagram doesn't add much clarity to the situation especially when the hot spot marking is only on one side of the 3 possible incursion points. In the meantime the best remedy is a reminder to be very vigilant when taxiing near runway intersections and always making sure to have the airport diagram pulled up on an EFB or printed out on paper however in this case that did not help me since my immediate focus was on safely vacating the runway I had just landed on."

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported confusing taxiway markings at ABQ led to a runway incursion.
narrative: While taxiing to Runway 26 via Alpha at ABQ; we mistakenly turned onto Taxiway A3 and crossed the hold short line for Runway 08/26 by a few feet. Captain immediately stopped the aircraft and reported to Ground. Ground acknowledged and subsequently cleared us to cross Runway 08/26 via A3 to continue our taxi.Cause: A loss of situational awareness occurred due to divided attention. I was distracted by a gate-departure logbook outage and further fixated on an unfamiliar; non-standard ramp marking near A3.Suggestions: As the PM; it is my responsibility to maintain strict situational awareness and actively cross-check our taxi route to back up the PF. However; I allowed the logbook outage and the unfamiliar ramp markings to divide my attention as well; failing to provide an effective backup. Additionally; having a note or description of the green oval marking on published charts would prevent crew confusion; as it remains highly distracting in its current state.
secondary_narrative: When departing ABQ; we were cleared to taxi to Runway 26 via Alpha. While taxiing we mistakenly turned onto Taxiway A3 leading to Runway 26-08. I noticed the mistake and immediately brought the aircraft to a stop; but by this time the aircraft was already a few feet past the hold short bars. I immediately advised ground that we mistakenly crossed the hold short bars of Runway 26-08. Ground acknowledged and a few moments later cleared us to cross Runway 26-08 via A3 and continue our taxi to Runway 26.Cause: I allowed unnecessary distractions to pull my attention away from the task at hand; taxiing the aircraft. We departed the gate during a logbook outage. Even though I complied as necessary with company logbook outage SOPs I still found myself running through the steps in the back of my mind as we began our taxi. Additionally there were nonstandard markings on the ramp abeam A3. A large green painted oval with yellow dashes. I had never seen this before and I was unsure if it was acceptable to taxi inside the green circle. Out of  precaution I taxied around it; but as I maneuvered the aircraft around the green circle I allowed myself to become fixated on it. It was at this time I lost situational awareness and made the wrong turn onto A3.Suggestions: As PIC it is required of me to focus 100% of my attention to the movement of the aircraft and not allow myself to become complacent in simple taxi instruction. Additionally it would be helpful there was a note or description of the painted green oval abeam A3 on published taxi charts. As of right now the markings are unclear and distracting.

synopsis: Corporate first officer reported conflict traffic taxied onto active runway resulted in rejected take off and a critical ground conflict.
narrative: Departing runway 28R full length at SFO we had a rejected takeoff due to Aircraft Y taxiing onto the runway in front of us. Aircraft Y had turned right on the 'E' taxiway onto the runway instead of left onto the taxiway per their taxi clearance. After we began our takeoff roll we noticed the runway safety lights illuminate red. In the few seconds between this and the time we processed the meaning of the lights ATC canceled our clearance and we aborted on the runway safely. Estimated speed at time of about was about 70; still within the low speed regime and we were able to quickly clear the runway onto taxiway N. The incursion by Aircraft Y also caused closely trailing traffic that was landing to have to go around. Crew discussed brake cooling and applicable procedures and due to low energy nature and very low takeoff weight determined that extended cooling times were not required. After reconfig; a short wait and brief the next takeoff was uneventful.What caused this -I can only speculate but it appeared they had been flying a long day with numerous legs so fatigue likely was a factor. How we could improve- There was a short period during the roll where the status lights had illuminated but we had not fully processed their meaning and applicable procedure. Likely due in part to lack of exposure to this system as Part 91 pilots mostly utilizing airports not so equipped.Recommend company safety bulletin on runway status lights and possibly integrating this scenario into sim training instead of the usual red hold short light scenario that training utilizes.

synopsis: Tower Controller reported a firefighting truck and associated vehicles crossed a runway they had been instructed to hold short of at the same time a departing aircraft was taking off.
narrative: Our facility is understaffed. We are allowed 12; 14 with training. We have 9; with 1 controller medically disqualified since the start of the busy season. Day 0 is the final day of the busy season. All our controllers are burned out. Everyone has been doing 6 day work weeks; lots of 10 hour days. Additionally in an attempt to get more staffing; our manager has increased our required time on position and reduced break times and lunch breaks. Moral of the story; we are burnt out. I had been fighting a cold or sickness of some sort and am not 100% at this time. I'm tired; I'm sick. I'm now in my 9th or 10th hour of work. The airport had an event on Day 0. There were several aircraft participating. Before the event; the aircraft altogether did about 100 separate ops in the traffic pattern; wearing out my supervisor and I; the only two there that morning. Luckily a third; fresh controller worked the event itself when he arrived to work at XA:15.During the event; all ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) units staged at Location X; which is across the airfield from the fire station. After the event was over; they called to relocate back to the fire station; needing to cross both parallel runways. My supervisor was working LC; at my request; as I was just so worn out and could barely talk or think anymore; that I felt I would only be safe on ground control; if that. So ARFF calls me and requests to cross both runways back to the fire station. At this time; Aircraft X is lining up to depart rwy XXL. I coordinate a conditional crossing reference the departing aircraft. My SUP approves the conditional.'ARFF and company; CROSS runway XX right at 1. HOLD SHORT runway XX left at 1.'I receive a perfect readback. I watch very carefully as the 3 ARFF units cross XXR. They get to the other side (Taxiway 2) and come to a full stop after clearing the runway. I literally nod my head and say to myself; that's what I want to see. I turn to watch this beautiful aircraft depart XXL and to know when it has passed Taxiway 1 so I can cross the ARFF units. Looks good; roaring down the runway. I make one last check on the ARFF units and turn my head toward them one more time. As my eyes see ARFF; I observe them moving fast (25-40 mph) across TWY 2. I key up the frequency and pretty much yell; 'ARFF; STOP!!!' The lead fire truck slams on it's breaks. I watch as the truck tips forward in its best attempt to stop. The other trucks also stop. ARF is over the hold short line. Seeing that they have all come to a complete stop; I quickly glance over to the aircraft to see if there is any way to cancel take off clearance. It is just airborne between taxiways 3 and 1. At this point; it was safer to let them takeoff. I clutch my chest because I literally can't fathom the thought of what had almost just occurred.The aircraft has now passed and I give the ARFF units clearance to cross runway XXL. I got off position quickly thereafter and left for the day.Recommendation: All of our controllers have had negative experiences with ARFF and how many mistakes on the airfield they have made. I love fire fighters; but these guys (and gals) need more training. The controller's have talked about having them over to the tower and giving them classes during our slow period; but it never seems to happen. Given incidents like this; perhaps the FAA can mandate some driver's tests or something for ARFF on the airfield.Nothing follows.

coded_anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: A pilot departing a non towered airport reported they observed a truck entering the runway at the same time they became airborne
narrative: The AWOS reported a temperature of 37 degrees Celsius; and a density altitude of 6300 feet. I have a personal limitation not to depart or land at an airport with a density altitude above 7000 feet in the Piper Tomahawk due to its limited performance. I communicated on the CTAF that I would be taxing for runway XX and performed all before-takeoff checks in the run-up area. A Cessna called on CTAF to announce it was on a 5 mile final. I announced I would be holding short of runway XX; and would plan to depart after traffic was clear of the runway. A few seconds later a King Air announces on CTAF that it will be overflying the runway to make left traffic for runway XX. I asked if they would be willing to extend their downwind; so that I could depart prior to their arrival without causing a traffic conflict. I mentioned how warm it was on the ground; and they agreed to build space in their pattern for me. Once the Cessna landed and called that they were clear of runway 29; I announced over the CTAF that I would be departing runway XX. I scanned for traffic on final; and for potential traffic conflicts on the 2 intersecting runways. Although the tall grass partially obscured the runways; it seemed clear. I began my takeoff roll; and noted how high the ground speed was before the airspeed was 'alive;' which I expected due the density altitude. I noticed two white pick-up trucks on a perpendicular taxiway; and assumed they would be holding short. I glanced inside to see I had achieved Vr; and when I looked outside to rotate; one of the pick-up trucks had started to cross the runway. Once I had realized what was happening; I was airborne and continued my takeoff. My best guess is that I rotated 2000' before the truck. The King Air; now on final called; 'hey ops; next time-if you're going to cross a runway; make a call. We have an airplane taking off and traffic on final!' The pick-up trucks had never made any calls on CTAF.I believe the heat; and my attention to the degraded performance of my plane due to density altitude narrowed my situation awareness. Had I widened my scan; I may have been able to identify the traffic conflict earlier; and rejected the takeoff. However; at the speed I was traveling when I did see the truck; I believe the best course of action was to fly the airplane away from the truck(which is what I did). The truck crossing a runway without communicating on CTAF was irresponsible and dangerous. Going forward I will be vigilant of not just other air traffic; but also ground vehicles. I was aware that non-towered airports may have air traffic that does not communicate using CTAF; but now I am aware that even ground vehicles may not participate in using the CTAF. I have learned from this experience to widen the scope of what threats to identify at non-towered airports.

synopsis: A flight instructor reported a NMAC while taking off from a non towered airport with an aircraft departing opposite direction.
narrative: An instrument student with a PPL and I were heading out for a cross country from our base ZZZ to ZZZ1 in a Vans RV-12. The other plane involved in this near miss was Aircraft Y. During the engine warm up after start my student noted that he thought Aircraft Y had perhaps landed on RWY XX at ZZZ. I surmised to my student that the 'Aircraft Y' had only back taxied on XX as we had just checked the AWOS and winds were reporting 210 at 7 Knots. The winds and traffic had been using runway XY. On top of this the wind sock looked 80% full straight down the pike for runway XY. We taxied to a runup area on the ramp and I noted another Aircraft Z in the pattern for runway XY. As we taxied on 1 we heard again Aircraft Z in the pattern for XY performing a Power Off 180. The timing of our taxi worked out that when we reached the departure end of XY we only waited briefly for the traffic to clear the runway. My student made the traffic call 'Aircraft X departing Runway XY left closed traffic departing off downwind'. We taxied onto runway XY and powered up. The runway has an elevated portion in the middle of it; as we accelerated and lifted off at the crest of the hill I then saw an airplane at the departure end of XX; which seemed to be moving. I immediately assumed controls and verbally transferred to me; I continued the climb and side stepped to the left as it seemed the airplane on the ground was drifting off centerline to the right. A quick scan of ADSB gave me his tail number and I sternly asked on the CTAF 'Aircraft Y are you up?!' The pilot of Aircraft Y responded. 'This is Aircraft Y...'Me 'Did you make that call that you were taking off?'Aircraft Y 'I did make a call that we saying we were taking off...'Me 'We did not hear that!'Me 'Did you hear us a call that we were taking off?'Aircraft Y 'No we did not hear you'Me 'What in the world?!'Other pilots in the area chimed in that they didn't hear either call.Aircraft Y 'OMG well sorry about that if I heard you were taking off I wouldn't have taken off'Me 'Also the winds are right down the pike.. on XY'Aircraft Y 'Oh I just saw Aircraft Z had landed; taxi I though he came in on XX'Me 'No; he just came in on a power off 180 for XY; we called our taxi and take-off...well all is well that ends well'On subsequent review of the the audio it was clear that we had both made the appropriate radio calls. And from my perspective there was very little either party could have done to mitigate the CTAF and miss-communication. Aircraft Y elected to take off downwind. The hill in the middle of the runway played a factor of us not hearing each others calls. In the future any Aircraft Y taxiing to their ramp area I will query when rwy XY is active.

Meanwhile Aircraft Y is now on final and continuing its approach while we are stationary on the runway waiting for Aircraft Z to take off. Actions we could have taken was to wait for Aircraft Z to go and for Aircraft Y to land; but as mentioned previously; we had clearly indicated our intention to use the runway surface well before Aircraft Y was on final approach; and before the Aircraft Z had indicated their intention to take off.

More fuel stops were made along the path.Arriving at Coeur d'Alene Lake; we toured for more photos and noticed the Sea Plane Base (S76) had two planes and a ferry boat docked and there was no room for another plane. We decided it would be best to fuel at COE; a non-towered airport shown on the current Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) sectional chart.After checking the AWOS at COE channel 135.075 for wind and other information; it favored Runway 20 for landing. With no additional comments; I switched to the UNICOM channel 122.8 as indicated on the sectional chart and announced my intentions five to six miles out that I was approaching and planned to overfly the airport 500 feet above the pattern altitude to verify the wind to Runway 20.During my approach; five miles out to the space COE; I did notice one aircraft departing to the west. Otherwise; there was no other traffic in the area after checking the windsock and verifying that Runway 20 was best wind for land. Also noticed there was no traffic in the air or on the ground. I announced that I was maneuvering for a mid-field crossing to enter left downwind; for Runway 20. After turning downwind; I made another radio call stating I was on an extended downwind for Runway 20. I lowered my landing gear and flaps; then announced I left base for Runway 20. I established a stabilized approach and announced final for Runway 20.Immediately after touching down; I heard a radio call about switching to 120 something? I exited the runway at the first taxi exit and headed for what I thought was the fuel area as there were Phillips 66 signs. Then I got a radio call asking my intentions. I responded that I needed some fuel. The controller told me that it was a towered airport now and I needed to switch to 120.125 frequency. I told him I had no idea as the current FAA chart indicates a non-towered airport with fuel. He said it was on the NOTAM and I made a mistake. He instructed me to taxi down to the run-up area of Runway 02 for further instructions. He told me that this has been a common miscommunication with pilots for a while.After fueling up for our last leg to ZZZ1; I called ATC for progressive taxi instructions to the tower for better explanation. The tower was a bit difficult to see or find as it was a makeshift setup of container boxes stacked up. After climbing to the top of containers where the controllers were; we had a nice cordial discussion regarding the lack of information available to incoming pilots. Not only is it not on the currently published sectional FAA charts; but it's also not on the NOTAM. The simple solution is to have it announced in the AWOS recording until the charts are updated. Additionally; the UNICOM channel should be monitored by ATC to give pilots the correct frequency as they enter the COE airspace and do not wait until after they have landed.Furthermore; I hope that your organization can be of some help to me in this particular case. As I take aviation responsibilities very seriously and don't want this to be a blemish on my record. I am not sure what I could have done differently except going to a different airport.In conclusion; I hope for the safety of all and the fairness of other pilots; the continuation ofthis problem at COE must be corrected; regardless of their growing pains.

synopsis: General aviation instructor reported a runway incursion at a non-towered airport when taking off without adequate spacing with an aircraft on final approach. The aircraft on final performed a go-around; which then conflicted with the instructor's aircraft during the climb.
narrative: My student and I planned to do a flight where we stayed in the pattern to practice landings. The incident happened at ZZZ; an uncontrolled airfield. On Departure; we lined up on Runway XX at ZZZ behind traffic executing a touch and go (a Cessna 172). A Experimental RV-10 was on final runway XX. I miss-judged the amount of spacing and time that we had to get off of the runway before landing traffic (Experimental RV-10) would be landing. I caused the Experimental RV-10 to go around as we took off. The Experimental RV-10 offset from the runway; and us; by only about 100-200 feet and was below us in altitude for around 10 seconds; they had around 20-30 knots of overtake speed on us; they accelerated ahead of us; then turned in front of us to the left for their left crosswind turn. Meanwhile there is still a Cessna 172 on the departure leg in front of me. The Experimental RV-10 turned left crosswind in front of me and behind the Cessna 172; essentially 'cutting off' the Cessna 172 who was about to turn crosswind in the pattern. The chain of events arose when I; the instructor; allowed our aircraft to take the runway when there was not enough space to takeoff before landing traffic. It was pure human error; and I realized as soon as we pulled onto the runway that there would not be enough space. In the future; I will continue to hold short of the runway if there is any doubt about whether there is enough space/time. Me pulling out and taking the runway when there was not enough time/space and 'cutting off' the RV-10 snowballed into the Experimental RV-10 'cutting off' a different plane in the pattern. Mistakes happen and I was the first to admit that I was at fault. The incident became a larger issue when the Cessna 172 revealed that they were on an FAA checkride. I essentially started the chain of events that led to the 'cutting off' of an airplane doing an FAA checkride with a Designated Pilot Examiner.

synopsis: BZN Tower Controller reported BZN Airport Operations has repeatedly published runway closure NOTAMs with inaccurate times. Reporter stated Operations also did not shut off the runway lights to indicate a runway was closed; leading to an aircraft nearly taking off the closed runway as the NOTAM had incorrectly stated it was still open.
narrative: I was the Control Tower Operator on duty for the evening shift. I ceased ATC operations at XA:30 and remained in the tower cab completing post-duty administrative tasks. I had been aware of the following NOTAM closing Runway 12/30 1 hour after the tower closed. No other runway closure NOTAM was ever issued concerning 12/30. While on the computer; I heard 2 transmissions on the CTAF. Both at/around XA:35. First; Aircraft X announcing they were taxiing out to Runway 30 for departure. And then a BZN Airport Ops person announcing that Runway 12/30; Runway 3/21; and a long list of taxiways were all closed. No response was heard from Aircraft X and they continued taxiing for departure; indicating they did not hear the advisory of the closures. Despite BZN Airport Operations having the ability to easily shut off and/or lock-out" runway/taxiway lights from the lighting vault; the runway lights for 12/30 remained on; in pilot control mode. The taxiway lights for the closed taxiways remained on too.BZN Airport Operations has repeatedly conducted the unsafe practice of purposely misrepresenting the time on a runway closure NOTAM by over an hour. This is not the first time this has occurred. Their intention almost always is to close 12/30 "after the arrival of the last scheduled air-carrier." However; since air carrier arrival times vary and since there is not a legitimate way to write a NOTAM saying that; they have 2 legitimate options. Either A: Issue a Prior Permission Required (PPR) style NOTAM; which they don't ever do because they are lazy and hate having to deal with phone calls/questions from flight crews and dispatchers coordinating PPRs. Or B: Wait until the last air carrier lands and then issue a standard runway closure NOTAM beginning at that time; with no advanced warning provided to pilots. They choose neither of those legitimate options and rather choose a shady middle ground where they issue a runway closure NOTAM hours or days in advance; but with the start time purposely set later than they actually intend on closing the runway. This gives flight crews known-false information; no advance notice regarding the real start time of the closure; and sets the flight crews up for failure. If flight crews are lucky; BZN Airport Operations waits until the last air carrier arrives; then cancels and reissues the NOTAM with the real start time and then calls Salt Lake Center informing them that they runway is closed time-now. That NOTAM reissuance did not happen tonight however. Per the NOTAMs; Runway 12/30 technically remained open during the incident.BZN Airport Operations has also repeatedly conducted the unsafe practice of failing/refusing to shut off the runway lights to a runway they just closed. Tonight was not the first instance of that either. I understand that the rule forbidding lighting a closed runway (JO7110.65BB 3-4-10-E) only applies to the control tower and does not restrict airport operations from doing so when the tower is closed; but continuing to light a closed runway when you don't have to is just stupid. It's a massive safety risk and one that was entirely unnecessary tonight. Had the runway lights for 12/30 been shut off; I am confident Aircraft X would not have attempted departure on that runway.Suggestions: 1. Issue PPR-style runway closure NOTAMS with the real/actual start time of the closure. Provide sufficient advance notice to aircrews. Grant PPRs as you see fit. 2. Shut off runway lights when closing a runway; if those lights aren't necessary for things like snowplowing or lighting maintenance. 3. FAA should codify (perhaps in an Advisory Circular (AC?)) suggestion #2 as it relates to airport operators when the ATCT is closed for the night."
